title: AI-ConneX Data Studio Data Profiler Detailed Documentation
summary: Statistical profiling SLAs, column distribution metrics, null ratio thresholds, and dataset exploration performance contracts.

sections.content:
AI-ConneX

Data Studio — Data Profiler

Proof of Concept • R&D • Technical Architecture • Manifest Generation

Industrial Data Intelligence LayerCompiler → Data Profiler → Manifest-UID.jsonStage Report / Compilation Report #1

The AI-ConneX Data Studio Data Profiler is the intelligence layer immediately after the Data Studio Compiler. The Compiler converts heterogeneous industrial source material into a validated, unified dataset. The Profiler then determines what the compiled dataset actually contains: its structure, semantics, statistical characteristics, quality indicators, relationships, temporal behavior, units, cardinality, distributions and suitability for downstream industrial AI workflows.

The Profiler also reconnects the technical facts discovered from the dataset with the intent established by the AI-ConneX Chatbot and the operational decisions made by the Compiler. These combined facts become a single machine-readable identity document called manifest-UID.json.

The key architectural idea is that a dataset is not considered fully understood merely because it has been normalized. The Compiler answers 'Can we make this data structurally usable?'; the Profiler answers 'What is this data, how does it behave, how reliable is it, and how does it relate to the user's industrial objective?'

sections.heading_text: 3.2 User Intent from Previous Chatbot Stage
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-003 > 3.2 User Intent from Previous Chatbot Stage
sections.content:
{  "intent_id": "ACX-INT-00042",  "industrial_domain": "manufacturing",  "objective": "predict machine failure",  "target_entity": "CNC machine",  "important_signals": ["temperature", "vibration", "motor_speed"],  "time_horizon": "next 24 hours",  "constraints": {    "preserve_source_context": true,    "explainability": "required"  }}

This intent is carried forward rather than discarded. It allows the Profiler to distinguish between generic data statistics and statistics that matter to the industrial objective.

The Profiler can also receive current-stage instructions. For example, an operator may ask it to identify candidate target variables, assess missingness in sensor streams, detect timestamp gaps, or determine whether a dataset is suitable for time-series forecasting.

{  "profiling_request": {    "mode": "industrial_full",    "check_time_series": true,    "check_sensor_quality": true,    "infer_relationships": true,    "generate_manifest": true  }}

The Profiler creates a unified context from three evidence streams:

The resulting manifest is therefore an operational data contract, not merely a profiling report.

sections.content: Traditional profiling tools generally answer generic questions: number of rows, columns, data types, null counts, unique values, descriptive statistics and distributions. Industrial AI-ConneX requires a broader concept of profiling because industrial datasets are usually temporal, sensor-driven, multi-asset, unit-dependent and purpose-specific.

How can the Profiler automatically characterize heterogeneous industrial variables after normalization?

How can generic statistics be transformed into industrially meaningful metadata?

How can the Profiler distinguish a useful sensor signal from an identifier, categorical label or administrative field?

How can time-series properties such as sampling frequency, gaps, irregular intervals and drift be detected automatically?

How can data quality be quantified without pretending that statistical quality equals engineering correctness?

How can the user's original objective influence which profiling checks receive priority?

How can the resulting metadata become a stable manifest that downstream AI-ConneX modules can consume?

Data profiling has a strong foundation in data quality, schema discovery, metadata management and data integration research. AI-ConneX extends this foundation by making profiling intent-aware and industrial-domain-aware.

Great Expectations provides a useful reference for the separation between expectations, validation and validation results; its current documentation describes validation definitions that associate data batches with expectation suites and return validation results. citeturn0search0turn0search2

Apache DataFusion is relevant to the proposed implementation because it uses Apache Arrow as an in-memory format and provides SQL/DataFrame APIs with support for CSV, Parquet, JSON and Avro, making it a viable high-performance analytical engine for profiling workloads. citeturn0search11turn0search14

sections.content:
For industrial sensor data, generic statistics are insufficient. The Profiler should additionally inspect:

Sampling interval and approximate sampling frequency.

Irregular timestamps.

Missing time windows.

Flat-line sensors.

Constant-value sensors.

Sudden spikes and discontinuities.

Out-of-range observations where engineering limits are known.

Sensor drift and distribution shift.

Noise indicators.

Unit consistency.

Machine/asset/channel cardinality.

Cross-sensor correlation and lag relationships.

Semantic profiling attempts to determine what a field represents, independently of its raw column name. The Profiler can combine canonical names from the Compiler, datatype, units, value ranges, naming patterns, metadata, and domain vocabulary.

Example:Column: temperatureType: floatUnit: °CRange: 21.2–94.7Context: CNC machineCorrelation: bearing_vibrationSemantic classification:asset_signal.temperaturemeasurement_type = temperatureengineering_domain = machine_health

A central AI-ConneX feature is that the Profiler does not treat all columns equally. If the user's objective is predictive maintenance, vibration, temperature, current, pressure and RPM may receive deeper analysis than an administrative operator ID.
tables:
| User Goal | High-Priority Profiling |
| --- | --- |
| Predictive maintenance | Sensor health, temporal continuity, anomalies, lag/correlation, target availability |
| Quality prediction | Process variables, batch identifiers, defect labels, leakage risks |
| Energy optimization | Power, current, load, runtime, energy-per-unit patterns |
| Production forecasting | Time index, production counts, seasonality, downtime, shift structure |
| Fault detection | Rare-event labels, anomaly patterns, sensor synchronization |

| Failure | Why It Happens | AI-ConneX Solution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Profiling only file structure | Generic tools stop at columns/types. | Industrial semantic + temporal profiling. |
| Wrong datatype inference | Mixed numeric/text values confuse inference. | Multi-pass type inference + confidence + sampling. |
| Missing values misunderstood | Null rate alone hides time gaps. | Separate cell-level missingness from temporal missingness. |
| Flat-line sensors missed | A column can be non-null but useless. | Variance, run-length and change-rate analysis. |
| Outliers treated as errors | Extreme values may be real machine events. | Context-aware anomaly classification; preserve evidence. |
| Correlations misunderstood | Correlation does not imply causation. | Label as association; never infer causality automatically. |
| Identifier mistaken for feature | High-cardinality columns can look informative. | ID detection and semantic classification. |
| Target leakage | Future/derived information may appear in features. | Intent-aware temporal and lineage checks. |
| Sampling mismatch | Sensors operate at different rates. | Per-signal frequency and synchronization profiling. |
| Unit inconsistency | Same semantic variable may contain different units. | Unit metadata + compiler lineage + conversion verification. |
| Profile becomes stale | Industrial datasets change over time. | Profile versioning and profile timestamps. |
| Too much metadata | Raw profiling can overwhelm downstream agents. | Tiered manifest: summary + detailed references. |
| LLM hallucination | Agent may invent semantics. | Evidence-backed semantic inference with confidence and provenance. |

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-003 > 15. How AI-ConneX Overcomes the Failures
sections.content:
Use deterministic computation for all numeric statistics.

Separate observed facts from inferred semantics.

Attach confidence and provenance to inferred metadata.

Preserve source and Compiler lineage.

Use domain-specific profiling policies.

Perform temporal checks for datasets containing timestamps.

Detect candidate identifiers before feature-quality scoring.

Never delete anomalies simply because they are statistically unusual.

Distinguish data-quality warnings from hard failures.

Version every manifest and profile execution.

Make the manifest reproducible from dataset hash + profile configuration + profiler version.

Use an agent only for interpretation and prioritization, not for arithmetic.

Every successful profiling run receives a Profile UID. The UID identifies the profile execution and allows downstream systems to distinguish different versions of the same underlying dataset.

Profile UID example:ACX-PROF-20260814-7F31A2C9Recommended identity inputs:dataset_hashcompiler_job_idprofile_config_hashprofiler_versionexecution_timestamp

The Profile UID should not replace the Dataset UID. Dataset identity, compilation identity and profiling identity should remain separately traceable.

After profiling, AI-ConneX merges the previous Chatbot intent, Compiler metadata and current Profiler findings. The resulting document is named using the manifest UID.

manifest-UID.json{  "manifest_uid": "ACX-MAN-00042",  "dataset": {    "dataset_uid": "ACX-IND-00042",    "artifact": "dataset.parquet",    "sha256": "..."  },  "intent": {    "intent_uid": "ACX-INT-00042",    "domain": "manufacturing",    "objective": "predict_machine_failure",    "target_entity": "CNC_machine"  },  "compiler": {    "compiler_job_id": "ACX-CMP-00042",    "status": "SUCCESS",    "schema_version": "1.0",    "lineage": "lineage.json"  },  "profile": {    "profile_uid": "ACX-PROF-20260814-7F31A2C9",    "profile_version": "1.0",    "rows": 999842,    "columns": 18,    "quality_score": 0.91,    "readiness": "CONDITIONALLY_READY"  },  "features": {    "high_relevance": [      "temperature",      "vibration",      "motor_speed"    ],    "candidate_target": "failure_event",    "candidate_time_index": "timestamp"  },  "quality": {    "null_rate": 0.012,    "duplicate_rate": 0.001,    "temporal_gaps": 4,    "anomaly_columns": 3  },  "next_stage": {    "recommended": "AI_DATA_PREPARATION",    "input_contract": "manifest-UID.json"  }}

sections.content:
The Profile Score is not a universal 'truth score'. It is a configurable operational score summarizing the observed fitness of the dataset for the stated intent.

Example weighted score:Quality              25%Completeness         20%Structural validity  15%Temporal integrity   15%Semantic confidence  10%Consistency          10%Intent suitability    5%Final = weighted score
tables:
| Score | Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.90–1.00 | READY | Strong candidate for downstream processing |
| 0.75–0.89 | CONDITIONALLY_READY | Usable with documented warnings |
| 0.50–0.74 | REVIEW_REQUIRED | Human/engineering review recommended |
| < 0.50 | NOT_READY | Major issues require remediation |

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-003 > 28. Compliance Report #1 — Data Profiler Stage

Compliance Report #1 is the formal evidence that the Data Profiler executed its defined checks and generated a traceable profile. It should not be interpreted as a legal certification by itself.

{  "report_id": "ACX-REP-PROF-00042",  "stage": "DATA_STUDIO_DATA_PROFILER",  "status": "SUCCESS",  "profile_uid": "ACX-PROF-20260814-7F31A2C9",  "input": {    "compiler_job_id": "ACX-CMP-00042",    "dataset_hash": "...",    "rows": 999842,    "columns": 18  },  "checks": {    "structural": "PASS",    "statistical": "PASS",    "quality": "PASS_WITH_WARNINGS",    "semantic": "PASS",    "temporal": "PASS_WITH_WARNINGS",    "relationships": "PASS"  },  "findings": {    "null_rate": 0.012,    "duplicate_rate": 0.001,    "temporal_gaps": 4,    "flatline_signals": 1,    "candidate_ids": ["machine_id"],    "candidate_target": "maintenance_event"  },  "score": {    "overall": 0.91,    "readiness": "CONDITIONALLY_READY"  },  "manifest": {    "manifest_uid": "ACX-MAN-00042",    "artifact": "manifest-UID.json"  }}

sections.content: CHATBOT  |  | intent_uid  | industrial domain  | objective  | constraints  vCOMPILER  |  | dataset_uid  | canonical schema  | transformations  | lineage  | validation  vPROFILER  |  | observed structure  | statistics  | quality  | semantics  | temporal behavior  | relationships  | intent relevance  vMANIFEST BUILDER  |  +-- chatbot intent  +-- compiler provenance  +-- profiler observations  +-- readiness score  +-- next-stage contract  vmanifest-UID.json

The Profiler does not overwrite the user's intent with what it discovers. It stores intent and observed reality as separate evidence layers. If the user asks for machine-failure prediction but the dataset contains no credible failure label, the manifest should say exactly that. The system should not invent a target variable.

intent.objective = "predict_machine_failure"profile.finding:  candidate_target = null  reason = "No validated failure-event label detected"manifest.readiness:  status = "REVIEW_REQUIRED"

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-003 > 32. Security, Governance and Compliance Design
sections.content:
Do not expose raw industrial data to an external LLM unless explicitly authorized.

Prefer sending schema summaries, samples or metadata to the agent rather than complete datasets.

Record which metadata was supplied to the agent.

Hash datasets and manifests for integrity.

Keep source artifacts immutable.

Use role-based access control.

Encrypt data in transit and at rest.

Separate tenant/customer namespaces.

Record profiler execution identity and configuration.

Maintain retention policies appropriate to industrial data.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-003 > 36. Suggested Research Paper Contribution Statement
sections.content: AI-ConneX Data Profiler proposes an intent-aware industrial data profiling layerthat combines deterministic structural/statistical profiling, temporal and sensorquality analysis, semantic inference, provenance from an upstream data compiler,and user-intent context into a unified machine-readable manifest.The approach separates observed dataset facts from inferred semantics and preserveslineage, confidence and reproducibility for downstream industrial AI workflows.

sections.content: The AI-ConneX Data Profiler converts a compiled dataset from a structurally usable artifact into an understood, contextualized and traceable data asset. Its most important output is therefore not the statistics themselves; it is the machine-readable manifest that preserves why the data exists, how it was compiled, what was discovered about it, how confident those discoveries are, and whether the dataset is suitable for the next AI-ConneX stage.

| Term | Definition |

| Dataset UID | Stable identity of the compiled dataset artifact. |
| Profile UID | Identity of one profiling execution/version. |
| Manifest UID | Identity of the merged intent + compiler + profile contract. |
| Intent | User/business/industrial objective supplied by the Chatbot. |
| Observed fact | A property directly measured from the dataset. |
| Inference | A semantic or contextual conclusion derived from evidence. |
| Confidence | Degree of support for an inferred property. |
| Lineage | Record of source and transformation provenance. |
| Readiness | Assessment of suitability for a specified downstream objective. |
